description: Team ASELTECH is a group of high school students from ASELSAN Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in Ankara, Türkiye. We started in robotics and finished 4th overall at the 2026 Micro Rover Challenge. Our members combine software, data analysis, 3D design and game development. We want to turn NASA’s open data into tools that are accurate, accessible and easy to understand, so anyone can experience the science behind our changing planet and beyond.
summary:
In many farming regions, wells pump groundwater out faster than rain can refill it. The clay underground compacts and the land above it sinks. This damage is permanent: canals and roads crack, and the aquifer can never store as much water again. It happens slowly, so most people never notice.

NISAR Vision, built by Team Aseltech, makes this hidden problem visible. We used the first data from NISAR, a new radar satellite from NASA and India’s space agency, ISRO, which can measure ground movement to the centimeter, day or night and through clouds.

In about 46 hours, we built an open system that turns raw radar data into clear numbers. Processing 168 pairs of radar images, we measured 20 sinking regions in 12 countries with the same method over the same 93 days, so they can be fairly compared. Eloy, Arizona, sinks fastest: 8.6 cm in just 100 days. About 370,000 people live on ground that sank more than 5 cm.

We made sure the numbers can be trusted. They closely match 10 GPS stations on the ground, and our automatic check even caught and fixed an error in our own top result. We turned the data into tools anyone can use: a 3D world atlas, a one-page report for each region for water managers, a simulator for testing pumping decisions, and Aquifer Run, a game that shows why sinking land matters. Everything is free and open-source.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

NISAR Vision is an end-to-end system that measures land subsidence, the slow sinking of the ground caused mostly by pumping too much groundwater. It turns those measurements into tools that water managers, scientists and the public can use.

It is built on the first months of provisional data from the new NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite. NISAR sends its own microwave pulses, so it can see the Earth’s surface day or night and straight through clouds. We compare pairs of radar images taken 12 to 24 days apart. The shift in the returning radar waves tells us how far the ground has moved. We correct for terrain using the Copernicus elevation model, drop unreliable pixels (coherence below 0.3), and convert the motion into vertical centimetres.

What makes our approach different is that we measured 20 basins in 12 countries with exactly the same method over exactly the same 93 days (28 June – 29 September 2026). Because every place was measured the same way, they can be compared fairly in one global ranking. Eloy, Arizona, sinks fastest at 8.6 cm in 100 days, followed by California’s Central Valley and Mexico City. Our system also checks itself automatically. It scans every time series for jumps of exactly one radar phase cycle (12.1 cm), a common processing error. That check caught a mistake in our own top result: Semarang first looked like the fastest-sinking city on Earth, but after the fix its rate fell from 12.1 to 6.2 cm.

What benefits does it have?

Our project connects raw space data with decisions on the ground. Its first benefit is early warning. Ground that sinks evenly does little harm. When it sinks unevenly, it tilts and cracks canals, roads and wells. We measured how steeply the ground tilts under 645 real canal and road segments in the Central Valley and found 81 at high risk, so repair crews know where to look first.

Its second benefit is trust. We compared our satellite results with 10 permanent GPS stations from the Nevada Geodetic Laboratory: they agree closely (r = 0.92, median error about 1 cm). Over Mexico City they also match NASA JPL’s independent OPERA product (r = 0.91). Every number on our site traces back to a data file in our open repository.

Its third benefit is a clear picture of the human and water cost. About 370,000 people live on ground that sank more than 5 cm. In the Central Valley alone, about 0.32 km³ of underground water storage is lost for good every year.

What is the intended impact of our project?

The intended impact is two-fold: protection and awareness.

For water managers and engineers, NISAR Vision works as a triage tool. Each basin has a printable one-page bulletin with its sinking speed, the people affected and its worst spots. Our open code can be run on any new basin with public NASA data.

For the public and decision makers, the impact is awareness. Groundwater loss is an invisible crisis: once clay layers are crushed, that storage never comes back. We built two experiences that make this visible. Our Groundwater Simulator lets anyone manage a real valley (Tulare Basin, USA, or Karapınar, Türkiye) for 24 months, starting from the sinking NISAR actually measured. Players balance farm income against permanent sinking, dry wells and canal damage. Aquifer Run, our browser and phone game, lets even children feel the problem: switch pumps off and the water underground refills, let it run dry and the ground sinks for good. Each level ends with the real NISAR rate for that valley.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use to develop our project?

On the data side, we used provisional Level-2 products from the NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite, accessed through NASA’s Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF DAAC). We used GUNW interferograms for ground movement and GCOV radar backscatter, together with NASA VIIRS optical imagery, to look beneath the clouds in the UK. For validation we used 10 Nevada Geodetic Laboratory GPS stations and NASA JPL’s OPERA product. We also used the Copernicus elevation model, OpenStreetMap for canals and roads, the European Commission’s GHSL 2025 population map, and NASA Blue Marble and NASA/JPL imagery for visuals.

The processing engine is written in Python, which makes up 59% of our code. It searches and downloads data with asf_search and reads NISAR files with h5py and rasterio. It computes with numpy and scipy, handles maps with pyproj and shapely, and draws charts with matplotlib. With one command it downloads and measures a region, checks every time series for phase-cycle errors and rebuilds the atlas. The website, the interactive 3D atlas and the simulator are written in JavaScript (28%), HTML (8%) and CSS (5%). They use MapLibre GL for maps, Chart.js for charts, KaTeX for formulas and satellite.js to show where NISAR is flying right now. Aquifer Run is written from scratch in JavaScript on an HTML canvas.

The site is hosted on GitHub Pages and Cloudflare Pages. Before every update, automatic checks confirm that the numbers are consistent and that no link is broken; the full test suite has 112 tests. The game can be installed on a phone like an app and is also published on itch.io. The whole project is open source under the MIT license.

We wrote code, analysis scripts and drafts with help from Anthropic Claude (Claude Code), Google Gemini and OpenAI Codex. The team reviewed everything, and every reported number comes directly from verified data files in the repository.

How is our project creative?

Most remote sensing projects stop at a coloured map. We went several steps further. We built one fair global ranking from the very first NISAR data, and we built an atlas that catches its own mistakes and shows them openly. We turned tilt measurements into a risk list for real canals and roads, and every basin got a one-page bulletin. We also made the science playable, with a decision simulator for adults and a game anyone can enjoy. All of it was built in about 46 hours, with 1,148 commits and 168 NISAR radar image pairs processed.

What factors did our team consider?

Scientific honesty and the limits of the data guided every decision. NISAR launched recently and its data are provisional, so we say on every page that calibration and validation are carried out by the NISAR project (NASA-JPL and ISRO), not by our team. We label each basin as reliable (9) or indicative (11). The radar measures motion along its viewing angle, so we report both that value and an estimated vertical value and explain the difference in plain words. Water vapour can mimic ground movement, so we documented the noise level and the differences from GPS. Farmers plough and flood their fields, which scrambles the radar signal. We treated those gaps as signs of active farming, not as failures, and used the stable edges of each basin to map the wider sinking area. Finally, we wanted judges, engineers, students and the public to understand the main message within minutes, so every page uses short sentences, real numbers and their sources.
